title: Search Suggestions System
pattern: sort once + lower-bound binary search over prefixes
statement:
A search box is fed a list of product names `products` and a `searchWord`. After the user types each character of `searchWord`, the box shows up to three suggestions.

Return a list of lists: the list at index `i` holds up to three names from `products` that start with the first `i + 1` characters of `searchWord`, chosen as the lexicographically smallest matches and sorted in ascending order. If fewer than three names match, return all of them; if none match, return an empty list, so a one-character `searchWord` produces exactly one list.

Names are lowercase words, comparisons are plain code-unit order, and a name that appears several times in `products` counts as several separate suggestions.

Constraints: `1 <= products.length <= 100` and `1 <= searchWord.length <= 20`.

constraints: Function signature: `function solve(products: string[], searchWord: string)`.
Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: The shape of the answer is fixed before any searching: one list per typed character, in order.
Sorting the names once puts every name that shares a prefix next to its neighbours, so the matches for any prefix form one contiguous block.

A lower-bound binary search finds the first name that is not smaller than the prefix; the three smallest matches start there, so walk forward at most three names and stop early if the prefix stops matching.

editorial.approach: The brute force redoes everything for every prefix: extend the prefix by one character, filter the whole product list with a linear prefix test, sort the survivors, take the first three. With `L` prefixes and `n` names that is O(L · n log n). The optimal sorts the products once with an explicit code-unit comparator, and then handles each prefix with a lower-bound binary search for the first name that is not smaller than the prefix. Names sharing a prefix occupy a contiguous block in sorted order, so the three smallest matches are the first three entries from that lower-bound index onward: one halving search plus at most three comparisons per prefix, for O(n log n + L log n) overall.
editorial.why_optimal: The single sort at O(n log n) is paid once and dominates; after that the only work per prefix is locating the block, which binary search does in O(log n). Nothing needs to be re-sorted or re-filtered, so the factor of `L` that the brute force pays disappears. With `products.length ≤ 100` both versions pass the judge easily, but the binary-search version is the one that still works when the catalogue has a hundred thousand names, which is what the sorting is really for.
editorial.pitfalls: Taking the first three names at the lower-bound index without re-verifying the prefix: the lower bound can land on a name that is merely greater than the prefix, for example `ac` for the prefix `ab`, so the three-item scan must stop at the first name that does not start with the prefix. Breaking out only on a strictly greater name, which keeps names that merely share the first character. Sorting with a comparator that does not match the comparison used by the binary search (a locale comparator, or numeric coercion), which silently breaks the contiguity invariant. And returning `L - 1` lists instead of `L`, or forgetting that a prefix with no matches still contributes an empty list.
